name: Photosynthetic pathways
what: This subtopic covers the process of photosynthesis, including the word and balanced chemical equations, the structure of the chloroplast, and the locations of the light-dependent and light-independent stages. It also covers autotrophs and the role of chlorophyll.
why: Photosynthesis is the process that converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, providing the foundation for almost all food chains. Understanding it is essential for explaining how energy enters living systems.

items.title: I can explain the function of chloroplasts
items.what: Chloroplasts are the organelles in plant and algal cells where photosynthesis occurs. They convert light energy into chemical energy by using carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen. Autotrophs are organisms that make their own organic materials this way, while heterotrophs must consume other organisms.
items.why: Understanding the role of chloroplasts links organelle structure to function and explains why plants are the primary producers in most ecosystems.
items.example: A leaf cell contains many chloroplasts because its primary function is photosynthesis. A root cell, which is underground and receives no light, does not contain chloroplasts and relies on glucose transported from the leaves.

items.title: I can draw a chloroplast and label its key structures and their functions
items.what: A chloroplast has a double membrane (outer and inner). Inside are grana (stacks of thylakoid membranes) where chlorophyll is located and the light-dependent stage occurs. The stroma is the gel-like fluid surrounding the grana, where the light-independent stage occurs. Chloroplasts also contain their own ribosomes and DNA, evidence of endosymbiosis.
items.why: Linking each structure to its function demonstrates deep understanding and is commonly assessed through diagram-based questions.
items.example: The thylakoid membranes are stacked into grana to maximise the surface area available for chlorophyll to capture light energy. More thylakoid membranes means more light can be absorbed and more photosynthesis can occur.

items.title: I can state the word equation and balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis
items.what: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water (with light energy and chlorophyll) produces oxygen + glucose. Balanced chemical equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O (with light energy and chlorophyll) produces 6O2 + C6H12O6. Light energy and chlorophyll must be written above or below the arrow, not as reactants.
items.why: Accurate recall of these equations is directly assessed in VCE Biology. Writing light energy and chlorophyll in the correct position shows you understand they are conditions for the reaction, not reactants consumed.
items.example: A common error is writing light energy as a reactant on the left side of the equation. The correct format places 'light energy' above the arrow and 'chlorophyll' below the arrow, indicating both are required conditions for the reaction to proceed.

items.title: I can summarise the inputs, outputs and location of the stages of photosynthesis
items.what: The light-dependent stage occurs on the thylakoid membranes (grana). It uses light energy and water, and produces oxygen. The light-independent stage occurs in the stroma. It uses carbon dioxide and produces glucose. Both stages are controlled by enzymes.
items.why: Being able to connect each stage to its location and its inputs and outputs is essential for answering multi-part exam questions about photosynthesis.
items.example: If you are asked where oxygen is produced during photosynthesis, the answer is the thylakoid membranes (grana) during the light-dependent stage. If asked where glucose is made, the answer is the stroma during the light-independent stage.
